findings.headline: Charts show billing above the documented level: 68% of 22 documented 99215s are below the billed level (peers 17%)
findings.interpretation: Billed 99215 on 25.4% of claims; the expected share for this panel is 2.6% (risk-adjusted z 16.75). The excess is on low-complexity patients: 21% of visits for patients with 0 chronic conditions were billed 99215, against 2.6% for all providers. A random sample of 30 (29 usable) plus a targeted 99215 sample found 20 of 44 charts below the billed level. The overpayment draft says it is not reliable (only 7 random 99215 charts, 8 needed), so no dollar figure is quoted. The targeted charts cannot be extrapolated. A certified coder should re-score the charts.

findings.headline: Highest 99215 share in the book (34%, expected 4%), also high on healthy patients; notes look inflated to match the bill
findings.interpretation: 28% of visits for patients with 0 chronic conditions and 31% for patients with 1 were billed 99215 (peers 2.6% and 3.8%). Few charts are documented below the billed level (2 of 29). But the notes show signs of being written up to match the claim: 38% address fewer problems than the billed level implies, 21% claim data review with no test on the claim, 24% are duplicates, 14% were signed late, and the audit trail shows 14% bulk-created and 21% paste-heavy. Note: the draft summary wrongly says no audit trail was received; one was received and it was used here. The overpayment draft says it is not reliable (too few 99213 charts), so no dollar figure is quoted. These signs are rates, not proof.

findings.headline: 99215 on 16–21% of visits for patients with 0–2 conditions (peers 3–6%) across 1,470 claims; notes show data review the claims don't support, plus audit-trail copy/paste signs
findings.interpretation: The first response was a billing ledger; after a follow-up, 30 random charts came back, plus 15 targeted 99215 charts. Only 1 of 44 charts is below the billed level, but 25% of notes claim data review with no lab or test line on the claim. 36% address fewer problems than the billed level, 25% are duplicates, 16% were signed late, and the audit trail shows 18% bulk-created and 20% paste-heavy. Hybrid review left this undecided. My leaning rests on the large excess of 99215s on low-acuity patients together with the note-inflation signs. A human should confirm this before any recovery.

findings.headline: Strongest note-inflation signs in the review, but a small practice with a modest claims excess
findings.interpretation: 99215 share is 18% against 3.6% expected, with 20% on patients with 1 condition. Only 1 of 30 random charts is below the billed level. Note signs are high: 27% claim data without tests, 40% duplicates, 23% signed late, and the audit trail shows 30% bulk-created and 30% paste-heavy. Honest practices also copy forward, and the excess is about $1.4k over 237 claims. A coder should look at these notes; recovery is not recommended on this evidence.

findings.headline: Strong claims outlier (risk-adjusted z 24.5; 21% 99215 on patients with 0 conditions) but no usable charts
findings.interpretation: The office sent a billing ledger and then did not answer the follow-up. The request was closed as non-responsive. Non-response is not evidence of upcoding. The claims pattern is still a strong reason for a human to decide on outreach.

findings.headline: Charts support the levels billed, but 99215 share is above expected on low-complexity patients
findings.interpretation: Across 45 charts (random plus targeted 99215), none were below the billed level. 49% of notes address fewer problems than the billed level implies, but the data and signature checks are clean. 99215 rate on patients with 0 conditions is 8% against 2.6%.
